vignette:
Erik is a thirty-two-year-old combat pilot who flies F-35s out of a base in the Southwest, a job he once loved for its precision and clarity. Nine months ago, after a squadron party, a fellow officer—someone Erik had trained with for years—sexually assaulted him in his own quarters. Erik never reported it. The man was a friend, a wingman; the betrayal felt absolute. In the weeks that followed, Erik began to scan the faces in the briefing room, certain that others knew, that they were watching him with silent judgment. He took to walking with his back to the wall. At home, a single-story rental near the flight line, he found himself lying awake at night, listening for footsteps on the gravel driveway, his heart hammering at the creak of the water heater. Ordinary sounds—a car door slamming, the clatter of a dropped tool in the hangar—made him flinch so hard that fellow pilots started to notice.

Erik had come to believe that his reactions proved he was a lousy coper. A combat pilot should be able to shake off anything. Instead, he felt hollowed out, his faith in people gone. He was certain that the assault had marked him as vulnerable, and that vulnerability made him a target. This conviction fed directly into his hypervigilance: because he had failed to protect himself once, he now had to monitor every unpredictable situation—the sudden appearance of a maintenance crew chief around a blind corner, an unannounced change in the flight schedule—for hidden threat signs. The more he watched for danger, the more danger he saw. A colleague’s casual glance across the tarmac became suspicious. A late-night engine test spooling up outside his window sent him scrambling to check the locks.

The loop tightened. Every time Erik startled at a harmless noise, he silently berated himself for being weak, which deepened his belief that he was a bad coper. And that belief made him even more hyperalert: he scanned the base commissary for men who stood too close, he listened for footsteps in the hallway during his off-hours, and he woke from nightmares with the residue of the assault still vivid, his body already braced for an attacker. The dream residue itself became a trigger—lying in the dark, disoriented, he would strain to hear if someone was actually in the house, and then lie rigid for an hour, afraid to move.

At work, Erik began to avoid the officers’ club and the squadron gym, where the perpetrator still trained. He requested a shift change that isolated him from the man, but the explanation he gave—"personal reasons"—raised eyebrows. His flight performance remained technically sound, but his crew chief noticed that Erik now did a full preflight check twice, as though he could not trust his own memory. The occupational consequence was subtle but real: he was passed over for a lead-instructor billet, his commanding officer citing "recent distractibility."

Erik finally sought help after a night when he woke from a nightmare, convinced he heard someone jimmying the lock, and spent forty-five minutes crouched behind his sofa with a service pistol aimed at the front door. The sun was rising before he could convince himself he was safe. What frightened him most, he told the intake clinician, was the feeling that the man who assaulted him was still in control—that even now, alone in his own home, he was still the one hiding. He wanted to stop jumping at shadows. He wanted to trust that the silence in his house was just silence. But he was terrified that, if he let his guard down, the betrayal would happen again.
